title: When to See a Gastroenterologist: Red Flags vs Routine Gut Symptoms
summary: Emergency signs first, then when gut symptoms call for a GI doctor.
body_markdown:
Some digestive symptoms settle on their own, while others need a specialist or emergency care. This guide is for US adults without a digestive diagnosis who are deciding when to see a gastroenterologist, the doctor who specializes in the digestive tract. It sorts warning signs into tiers, from emergency care to a first conversation with primary care, using guidance from US health agencies and gastroenterology societies. It cannot assess your symptoms, so call a clinician if you are unsure. If you already have Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, read the guide on[when to call your GI, visit urgent care or go to the ER](https://aidyhq.com/learn/when-to-call-your-gi-visit-urgent-care-or-go-to-the-er-for-ibd-symptoms) instead.


## Get emergency care now if you have these symptoms


The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) lists[signs of acute gastrointestinal bleeding](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/gastrointestinal-bleeding/symptoms-causes) that need medical help right away: vomiting blood, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, black or tarry stool, and blood mixed with stool, along with fainting, dizziness or shortness of breath. It says signs of shock, such as confusion, a fast heart rate, pale skin, cold hands and feet, or sweating, need emergency help right away. MedlinePlus, from the National Library of Medicine, advises[getting help right away or calling 911](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003120.htm) for abdominal pain with any of these:


- sudden, sharp pain, or a belly that is rigid or tender to the touch
- vomiting blood, or blood in the stool that is bright red, maroon or black
- being unable to pass stool, especially while vomiting


MedlinePlus also lists abdominal pain during pregnancy, after an abdominal injury, or spreading to the chest, neck or shoulders. A specialist visit can follow once you are stable. If you cannot tell whether symptoms are severe enough, the standard advice is to call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.


## Symptoms that need a doctor right away


Other symptoms call for contacting a clinician promptly. NIDDK advises adults to[talk with a doctor right away](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/diarrhea/symptoms-causes) for diarrhea lasting more than 2 days, six or more loose stools a day, high fever, frequent vomiting, severe abdominal or rectal pain, stools that are black and tarry or contain blood or pus, a change in mental state, or signs of dehydration such as extreme thirst, urinating less than usual, dark urine or dizziness. NIDDK adds that people who are pregnant, over 65, taking antibiotics or immunocompromised should stay in touch with their doctor during diarrhea. For constipation, NIDDK says to[see a doctor right away](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/symptoms-causes) if it comes with rectal bleeding, blood in the stool, constant abdominal pain, inability to pass gas, vomiting, fever, lower back pain, or weight loss you were not trying for. The 2-day mark is a prompt to call, separate from the definition of chronic diarrhea.


## Symptoms that are a reason to see a gastroenterologist


Referrals usually follow symptoms that persist or suggest bleeding or inflammation. NIDDK defines[chronic diarrhea as lasting at least 4 weeks](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/diarrhea/definition-facts) , and the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA)[guideline on chronic diarrhea](https://gastro.org/press-releases/aga-releases-guideline-on-the-evaluation-of-chronic-diarrhea-1/) recommends testing at that point for celiac disease and the parasite Giardia, with a stool test such as fecal calprotectin suggested to screen for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) advises seeing a doctor[right away for blood in the toilet or stool](https://gi.org/topics/colorectal-cancer/) , abdominal pain or constipation, low blood counts or iron, and weight loss. Iron deficiency anemia is a reason for a GI workup in its own right: the AGA[recommends upper and lower endoscopy](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/) for men and postmenopausal women with it and conditionally suggests the same for premenopausal women. For constipation without warning signs, NIDDK suggests[seeing a doctor when symptoms do not go away with self-care](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/constipation/symptoms-causes) , or if you have a family history of colon or rectal cancer.


## When primary care is the right first step


A primary care clinician is often a practical place to start. When irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is suspected, NIDDK says[doctors review symptoms and medical and family history and perform a physical exam](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) , and may order blood or stool tests for anemia, infection or other disease. The ACG guideline on IBS recommends a[positive diagnostic strategy built on a careful history, a physical exam and limited testing](https://webfiles.gi.org/docs/publications/ibs_guideline_acg_magazine.pdf) , including tests to rule out celiac disease and IBD when IBS with diarrhea is suspected. If results or symptoms point beyond IBS, the next step is usually a gastroenterology referral. Seeing primary care first is not a medical requirement, and whether you need a referral depends on your insurance. HealthCare.gov notes that[many HMO plans require a referral from your primary care doctor](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/referral/) before you see another provider and may not cover the visit without one, so check your plan before booking a specialist directly.


## Family history and colorectal cancer screening


The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)[recommends screening adults aged 45 to 75](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/colorectal-cancer-screening) and selectively offering it from 76 to 85, and ACG[recommends starting at 45 for people at average risk](https://gi.org/topics/colorectal-cancer/) . The USPSTF recommendation covers only adults without signs or symptoms of colorectal cancer, and it excludes people with IBD, a past colorectal cancer or adenomatous polyps, or a hereditary syndrome such as Lynch syndrome. Someone with bleeding, anemia or weight loss falls outside screening guidance at any age and needs a diagnostic evaluation.[ACG's patient page](https://gi.org/topics/colorectal-cancer/) adds that if a parent, sibling or child had colon cancer or a precancerous polyp, screening generally begins at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest affected relative's age at diagnosis, whichever is younger. Confirm the repeat schedule with a gastroenterologist. People already diagnosed with IBD follow a colonoscopy schedule set by their GI team.


## Could it be IBS or IBD?


People asking when to see a gastroenterologist for IBS often want to know whether symptoms could be inflammatory. NIDDK describes IBS as[abdominal pain often related to bowel movements plus changes in bowel habits](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/symptoms-causes) and says it does not damage the digestive tract. A doctor may diagnose IBS when symptoms have occurred at least weekly for 3 months and began at least 6 months earlier, though[NIDDK says a diagnosis can come sooner](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . Ulcerative colitis, a form of IBD, commonly causes[diarrhea, rectal bleeding, mucus or pus in the stool, and sudden urgency](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/ulcerative-colitis/symptoms-causes) , and it sometimes runs in families. NIDDK lists anemia, rectal bleeding, black or bloody stools, weight loss and a family history of celiac disease, colon cancer or IBD as[signs that may point](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) to a problem other than IBS. ACG[advises against routine colonoscopy](https://webfiles.gi.org/docs/publications/ibs_guideline_acg_magazine.pdf) in people under 45 with IBS symptoms and no warning signs such as unintentional weight loss, older age at onset or a relevant family history. See[IBS vs IBD red flags and tests](https://aidyhq.com/learn/ibs-vs-ibd-key-differences-red-flags-and-the-tests-doctors-use) for more.


## What to track before your appointment


Notes made before the visit make your history more accurate. Record when symptoms started, how often they occur, your usual number of bowel movements a day, and whether stools contain blood, mucus or pus, since the thresholds above depend on those details. Note weight change, fever, symptoms that disrupt sleep, and your medicines, including recent antibiotics. Write down any family history of colon cancer, polyps, IBD or celiac disease, with each relative's age at diagnosis if you know it. Bring recent blood test results, particularly a blood count or iron level. A food and symptom diary kept for a week or two covers most of this. Readers already diagnosed with IBD can use an[IBD flare action plan](https://aidyhq.com/learn/ibd-flare-action-plan-what-to-track-who-to-call-and-when-to-seek-urgent-care) to decide what to track and whom to call.


In short, heavy bleeding, shock or sudden severe abdominal pain need emergency care. Diarrhea beyond 2 days, blood or pus in the stool, high fever or dehydration need a clinician right away. Chronic diarrhea, iron deficiency anemia, unexplained weight loss or a relevant family history are reasons to see a gastroenterologist, often through primary care. Screening at 45, or earlier with family history, is for people without symptoms.


This article is for educational purposes and is not medical advice. It is researched against current AGA clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources. Always discuss treatment decisions with your care team.
